profile.feeling: Agreement and confirmation; as a little modal word, “as you know”.

senses.def: yes (answer to a question)
modal particle: as we know, after all, obviously (Das ist ja toll!)

examples.tr: Do you like tomatoes? – Yes, very much!

phrases.meaning: to say “I do” – to marry someone

synonyms.nuance: emphatic “yes, sir” – military or very deferential; also ironic
exactly, right – agreement in conversation
yes – but ONLY as the answer that contradicts a negative question or statement

etymology.text: From Middle High German ja, from Old High German ja, jā (“yes”), from Proto-Germanic *ja (“yes”). Cognate with Yiddish יאָ (yo).

funFacts: The famous unstressed ja in the middle of sentences (Du bist ja nass!) is one of the German modal particles that have no direct English equivalent.
pitfalls: Answering a negative question with ja is ambiguous: Magst du keine Tomaten? – Doch! (Yes, I do.) / Nein. (No, I don't.)
subtleties: Mid-sentence, unstressed ja is not “yes” but a modal particle that marks something as obvious or surprising.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses nein as “no”; the concept gloss “no (the answer)” has no other word the check can find.

profile.feeling: A clear refusal or denial – softened with danke.

senses.def: no (answer to a question)
exclamation of surprise or disbelief (Nein, wirklich?)

examples.text: Willst du noch Kaffee? – Nein, danke.
examples.tr: Do you want more coffee? – No, thank you.

examples.text: Nein, das ist keine Gurke, das ist eine Zucchini.
examples.tr: No, that's not a cucumber, it's a zucchini.

examples.text: Nein! Wirklich? Das glaube ich nicht.
examples.tr: No! Really? I don't believe it.

synonyms.nuance: relaxed spoken “nope”, very common in northern and central Germany
casual, slightly cheeky “nah”

etymology.text: From Middle High German nein, from a contraction of Old High German ni ein (“not one”). Compare Old English nān, from ne ān (Modern English none, further contracted to no).

funFacts: nein literally means “not one” – the same pattern as English none (ne + one).
pitfalls: nein answers a question; inside a sentence the negation is nicht or kein: Ich mag keine Zwiebeln (not *Ich mag nein Zwiebeln).
subtleties: To contradict a negative statement you say doch, not ja: Du magst keinen Spinat. – Doch!

profile.feeling: The all-purpose hello – friendly, everyday, also on the phone.

senses.def: hello, hi – greeting when you meet someone (informal to neutral)
hello – answering the phone or calling for attention (Hallo? Ist da jemand?)
Hallo?! – disbelief or protest (“excuse me?!”)

synonyms.nuance: the polite daytime greeting for strangers and at work
from English; young people, messages
the usual greeting in Bavaria and Austria, polite (lit. “God greet [you]”)
hello and goodbye among friends in Bavaria and Austria
hello at any time of day in northern Germany
the polite hello in Switzerland

etymology.text: Originally used as a call to the ferryman on the other side of the bank; related to Old High German holā, emphatic imperative of holōn (“to fetch, used especially in hailing a ferryman”). Also see French holà (“hey! stop!”).

funFacts: hallo began as a shout to call the ferryman across a river: holā! = “fetch (me)!”.
pitfalls: Hallo is fine with friends, colleagues and most young people; with an older stranger, in an office or in a formal letter use Guten Tag (letters: Sehr geehrte Frau …).
subtleties: On the phone many Germans answer with their surname (Weber?) rather than Hallo.
Hallo works at any time of day; Guten Morgen / Tag / Abend depend on the hour.

profile.feeling: Polite and correct – the greeting for shops, offices, strangers and older people.

senses.def: hello, good day, good afternoon – polite greeting from late morning to early evening

examples.text: Guten Tag, ich hätte gern zwei Brötchen.
examples.tr: Hello, I’d like two bread rolls, please.

examples.text: Er sagt nicht einmal guten Tag.

synonyms.nuance: short form in relaxed speech
polite greeting in the south and in Austria
friends, colleagues, young people

etymology.text: Short for ich wünsche einen guten Tag! (“I wish [you] a good day!”), hence the accusative form of the adjective. Compare Yiddish אַ גוטן טאָג (a gutn tog).

funFacts: The Yiddish greeting a gutn tog is the same formula.
pitfalls: guten, with -en: it is an accusative (einen guten Tag wünschen), never *gute Tag.
Guten Tag greets; to wish a good day when leaving say Schönen Tag noch!
subtleties: In southern Germany and Austria Grüß Gott is more usual than Guten Tag; in the north Moin.
In casual speech it shrinks to Tag! or Tach!

profile.feeling: The first greeting of the day – at home, at work, in the bakery.

senses.def: good morning – greeting until about 10–11 a.m.

examples.text: Guten Morgen! Hast du gut geschlafen?
examples.tr: Good morning! Did you sleep well?

examples.text: Guten Morgen zusammen! Ist noch Kaffee da?
examples.tr: Good morning, everyone! Is there any coffee left?

collocations.tr: to say good morning to someone

synonyms.nuance: short form among colleagues and family
northern German hello at any time of day

etymology.text: guten (masculine accusative of gut, “good”) + Morgen (“morning”), as in ich wünsche einen guten Morgen. Compare Yiddish גוט־מאָרגן (gut-morgn).

funFacts: Moin looks like a short form of Morgen, but Wiktionary calls its origin unclear – and it is used even at night.
pitfalls: Accusative guten, like guten Tag and guten Abend.
der Morgen = the morning, but morgen (small m) = tomorrow: Bis morgen! = See you tomorrow.
subtleties: Colloquially just Morgen! – in northern Germany Moin is said all day, not only in the morning.

profile.feeling: Arriving in the evening: a restaurant, a visit, the news on TV.

senses.def: good evening – greeting when you meet someone from about 6 p.m.

examples.text: Guten Abend, haben Sie einen Tisch für zwei?
examples.tr: Good evening, do you have a table for two?

examples.text: Guten Abend, meine Damen und Herren!

collocations.tr: to say good evening to someone

synonyms.nuance: short form
any time of day, among friends

etymology.text: By surface analysis, guten (masculine accusative of gut (“good”)) + Abend (“evening”).

funFacts: The 8 p.m. television news, the Tagesschau, traditionally begins with Guten Abend, meine Damen und Herren.
pitfalls: Guten Abend is said when you arrive or meet; when you leave in the evening say Schönen Abend noch! or Gute Nacht (late).
subtleties: Like guten Tag it is an accusative of wishing: (ich wünsche einen) guten Abend.

profile.feeling: Bedtime, parting late at night.

senses.def: good night – said when going to bed or parting late at night
Na dann gute Nacht! – “then we’re done for / forget it”

examples.text: Wenn der Zug ausfällt, na dann gute Nacht!
examples.tr: If the train is cancelled, then we’ve had it!

collocations.tr: to say good night to someone

phrases.meaning: then all is lost / that will never work

synonyms.nuance: sleep well – to family and friends
short form

funFacts: Brahms’s lullaby begins Guten Abend, gut’ Nacht – with the old short form gut’ Nacht.
pitfalls: gute, not *guten: Nacht is feminine (die Nacht), so the accusative ending is -e, while Tag, Morgen and Abend are masculine (guten).
Never a greeting on arrival – at 11 p.m. you still arrive with Guten Abend.
subtleties: Children often hear the rhyme Gute Nacht, schlaf gut, träum was Schönes!

profile.feeling: The polite goodbye – shops, offices, people you say Sie to.

senses.def: goodbye – polite (lit. “until we see each other again”)

examples.tr: Thank you very much and goodbye!

synonyms.nuance: bye – friends, family, and today often in shops
short form
goodbye in Swabia and the south-west

etymology.text: Literally, “until our reunion; that we may see again”. Probably a calque of French au revoir. Compare Italian arrivederci, Dutch tot ziens.

funFacts: Auf Wiederhören is a German speciality: a goodbye that only works on the phone or radio.
pitfalls: On the phone you cannot “see again”: say Auf Wiederhören (“until we hear each other again”).
Wiedersehen (to see again) is written with ie; wider (against) has no e.
subtleties: Auf Wiedersehen is polite but not cold: shop staff say it to every customer. With friends it sounds stiff – use Tschüss.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses tschüss as “bye, cheers, ciao” – the informal goodbye; the check looks for the word “goodbye”.

profile.feeling: The everyday bye – warm, quick, used by almost everyone.

senses.def: bye, cheers, ciao – informal goodbye

synonyms.nuance: the polite goodbye
from Italian, very common
bye (and hello) in Bavaria and Austria
bye in Swabia and the south-west

etymology.text: Borrowed from German Low German tschüß from earlier adjüs, from Dutch adjuus, from Spanish adiós or French adieu. (Compare the origin of moin.)

funFacts: tschüss is a distant cousin of Spanish adiós and French adieu – “(I commend you) to God”.
pitfalls: Spelling: tschüss and tschüs are both correct; tschüß is the old spelling.
subtleties: Once northern, tschüss is now used all over Germany, and in shops it is often neutral rather than informal; in the south people also say Servus, Ade or Pfiat di.

profile.feeling: See you in a little while – the same day.

senses.def: see you later (the same day)

examples.tr: I’m going shopping – see you later!

synonyms.nuance: till then – a time already agreed
see you in a moment (minutes)

pitfalls: bis später is for the same day; for another day say bis bald, bis morgen or bis dann.
subtleties: bis + a time word makes many goodbyes: bis morgen (tomorrow), bis Montag, bis dann (till then).

profile.feeling: See you soon – a friendly goodbye with no date fixed.

senses.def: see you soon

examples.text: Danke für den Abend, bis bald!
examples.tr: Thanks for the evening, see you soon!
Best wishes and see you soon!

synonyms.nuance: later the same day
until next time

pitfalls: bald means soon, not bold: bis bald = see you soon.
subtleties: bis bald often closes friendly e-mails and messages, after Viele Grüße.

override.pos: Wiktionary files wie geht’s as a “phrase”; a greeting formula is an interjection (INTJ) in this course.

profile.feeling: The quick friendly “how are you?” – an answer is expected, but a short one.

senses.def: how are you? how’s it going? (short, informal)

examples.text: Na, wie geht's? – Gut, und dir?
examples.tr: Well, how’s it going? – Fine, and you?

synonyms.nuance: the full form, to one person you say du to
the polite form
all good? – very casual

etymology.text: From wie geht es dir. Literally, “how does it go?”; compare English how's it going?, French comment ça va?.

funFacts: French ça va, Greek τι κάνεις and Russian как дела? ask the same thing in other images: going, doing, affairs.
pitfalls: Spelling: wie geht's (apostrophe for the dropped e of es); wie gehts without it is also allowed.
subtleties: Wie geht's? is a real question: Germans often give a real answer (Ganz gut, ein bisschen müde …) – it is not just “hi”.
It is neutral enough to use with colleagues you say Sie to; the full formal question is Wie geht es Ihnen?

override.pos: Wiktionary files wie geht es dir as a “phrase”; a greeting formula is an interjection (INTJ) in this course.

profile.feeling: How are you? – to a friend, a child, someone in the family.

senses.def: how are you? (to one person you say du to)

examples.text: Hallo Oma, wie geht es dir?
Lange nicht gesehen! Wie geht es dir?
examples.tr: Long time no see! How are you?

synonyms.nuance: the polite form (Sie)
short form

pitfalls: dir (dative), not *du: the person goes in the dative – es geht mir gut (I am fine), wie geht es dir?
To several friends: Wie geht es euch?
subtleties: es geht + dative is how German talks about how someone is: Mir geht es gut, ihm geht es schlecht.

override.pos: Wiktionary files wie geht es Ihnen as a “phrase”; a greeting formula is an interjection (INTJ) in this course.

profile.feeling: How are you? – polite and respectful.

senses.def: how are you? (polite: to one or several people you say Sie to)

examples.text: Guten Tag, Herr Doktor, wie geht es Ihnen?
Danke, gut. Und wie geht es Ihnen?
examples.tr: Fine, thanks. And how are you?

synonyms.nuance: to one person you say du to
short, relaxed form

etymology.text: Literally, “how is it going for you”.

pitfalls: Ihnen with a capital I = you (polite); ihnen = them: Wie geht es ihnen? = How are they?
The answer returns the question: Danke, gut. Und Ihnen?
subtleties: A doctor asking Wie geht es Ihnen? wants to know about your health – it can be a real medical question.

override.meaning: The concept is the answer “fine, well” (Gut, danke. / Mir geht es gut.); Wiktionary’s adjective gives “good; all right, satisfactory” and its adverb gut “well” – one word in German.

profile.feeling: Fine, good, well – the answer to Wie geht’s? and one of the most frequent German words.

senses.def: fine, well – how someone is (Gut, danke. / Mir geht es gut.)
good (quality, morals, taste): ein gutes Buch
Gut! – okay, all right (agreement)

examples.text: Wie geht es Ihnen? – Gut, danke.
Mir geht es heute nicht so gut.
examples.tr: I’m not feeling so well today.

examples.text: Gut, dann machen wir es so.
examples.tr: Okay, then we’ll do it that way.

phrases.meaning: all the best – for birthdays and farewells

synonyms.nuance: great, fine – cheerful
great – enthusiastic
all right, okay – about things more than feelings

antonyms.note: bad; Mir geht es schlecht = I feel bad / ill

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German guot, from Old High German guot, from Proto-West Germanic *gōd, from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to unite, be associated, suit”). Cognate with Dutch goed, English good, Danish god, Swedish god.

funFacts: gut is the same word as English good and Dutch goed; Guten Tag is literally “good day”.
German school marks run from 1 (sehr gut) to 6 (ungenügend); 2 is gut.
pitfalls: How you are is Mir geht es gut (dative mir!), not *Ich bin gut – that means “I am good (at something / a good person)”.
Irregular comparison: gut – besser – am besten.
subtleties: German uses one word for good and well: Er singt gut (he sings well).
Before a noun it takes endings (ein guter Freund, eine gute Idee); after sein it does not (Das Buch ist gut).
The answer ganz gut means “okay, not bad” – less than gut.

profile.feeling: Names and meanings: Ich heiße …, Wie heißt das auf Deutsch?

senses.def: to be called, to have the name (Ich heiße Anna = my name is Anna)
to mean (Was heißt das? Nein heißt nein.)
das heißt (d. h.) – that is, i.e.
to bid, to tell (someone to do something): jemanden willkommen heißen

examples.text: Hallo, ich heiße Maria. Und wie heißt du?
examples.tr: Hi, my name is Maria. And what’s your name?
What is that called in German?

examples.text: Wir kommen am Montag, das heißt in drei Tagen.
examples.tr: We’re coming on Monday, that is in three days.

phrases.meaning: a refusal must be respected – also the principle of the German sexual-offence law reform of 2016

synonyms.nuance: my name is … – more official, on the phone or in a meeting
to call oneself – a chosen name, a title
to mean – for words and signs (sense 2)

etymology.text: From Middle High German heiȥen, from Old High German heiȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *haitan, from Proto-Germanic *haitaną. Cognate with Yiddish הייסן (heysn), Dutch heten, Old Norse heita, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (haitan); compare also English hest, behest.

funFacts: Old English had the same verb: hātan, “to be called” – it survives only in the archaic English hight (“named”).
pitfalls: du heißt, not *heißst: the ending -st loses its s after ß (as after s, z: du sitzt).
Asking a name uses wie (how), not was: Wie heißt du? (not *Was heißt du?).
Strong verb: hieß (preterite), geheißen (participle).
subtleties: Ich heiße Anna is the everyday way; Mein Name ist Anna sounds more official; Ich bin Anna is casual.
In Switzerland it is spelled heissen (no ß).

profile.feeling: Nice to meet you – said with a handshake when you are introduced.

senses.def: nice to meet you, pleased to meet you (said when introduced)

examples.text: Das ist meine Kollegin Eva. – Freut mich!
examples.tr: This is my colleague Eva. – Nice to meet you!

synonyms.nuance: very pleased – rather old-fashioned
pleased to meet you – old-fashioned, said with a handshake
nice to meet you (du)

pitfalls: The answer is Freut mich auch! or Mich auch! (“me too”).
Without kennenzulernen it can also mean “I’m glad” in general: Das freut mich! = I’m glad to hear that.
subtleties: It is short for Es freut mich (, Sie kennenzulernen): “it pleases me”, with es dropped – mich is the accusative of ich.

profile.feeling: Gratitude – said all the time, and also the polite way to say no.

senses.def: thanks, thank you
(Nein,) danke – no, thank you: declining an offer

examples.tr: Thank you very much! – You’re welcome.

synonyms.nuance: many thanks – the safe polite choice, also in writing
thank you very much – warm
I thank you – speeches, letters
thanks – everyday in Switzerland

etymology.text: Ellipsis of ich danke dir (“I thank you”).

funFacts: danken (to thank) and denken (to think) are related – just like English thank and think.
pitfalls: A bare Danke! when someone offers you something often means “no, thanks”. To accept, say Ja, bitte! or Ja, gern!
danke für + accusative: Danke für den Kaffee.
subtleties: Formal: Ich danke Ihnen / Vielen Dank; warm: Danke schön; casual: Danke dir!

profile.feeling: The little word of politeness: please, you’re welcome, here you are, pardon?

senses.def: please (in a request or an offer)
you’re welcome (answer to danke)
Wie bitte? / Bitte? – pardon? sorry? (asking someone to repeat)
here you are (Bitte schön! when handing something over)

examples.text: Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe. – Bitte schön, gern geschehen.
examples.tr: Thank you very much for your help. – You’re very welcome.

examples.text: Wie bitte? Ich habe Sie nicht verstanden.

collocations.tr: you’re very welcome; here you are

synonyms.nuance: you’re welcome – “it was gladly done”
you’re welcome, my pleasure – short and friendly
no problem – casual answer to thanks
don’t mention it

funFacts: bitte is the verb bitten (“to ask, request”), cut down from ich bitte; English bid (“to ask, to pray”) is its cousin.
pitfalls: One word for two English ones: bitte = please AND you’re welcome.
To ask someone to repeat, say Wie bitte? – a bare Was? sounds rude.
subtleties: bitte goes almost anywhere in a request: Bitte setzen Sie sich! / Setzen Sie sich bitte! – mid-sentence it sounds softer.
Bitte schön / bitte sehr are warmer than bitte alone.

profile.feeling: Small slips and polite interruptions: sorry! – excuse me!

senses.def: sorry! (a small apology)
excuse me (to get attention or to get past)

examples.text: Oh, Entschuldigung! Das war mein Fehler.
examples.tr: Oh, sorry! That was my mistake.
Excuse me, where is the station?
Excuse me, may I get past?

synonyms.nuance: excuse me – polite verb form to a stranger
pardon me – a little more formal and old-fashioned
from English, very common among young people
I’m sorry – real regret or sympathy

funFacts: ent- (away) + Schuld (guilt): to entschuldigen someone is literally to take the guilt away.
pitfalls: For real regret, bad news or sympathy, Entschuldigung is too light: say Es tut mir leid.
Written with a capital E: it is a noun (die Entschuldigung, “apology, excuse”) used as an exclamation.
subtleties: As a noun, die Entschuldigung is also an excuse and a note from parents for missing school.
Entschuldigen Sie (bitte)! is the more polite way to stop a stranger.

override.pos: Wiktionary files es tut mir leid as a “phrase”; as a fixed formula of apology it is an interjection (INTJ) in this course.

profile.feeling: Real regret and sympathy: I’m sorry.

senses.def: I’m sorry (apology, regret; also sympathy: I’m sorry to hear that)

examples.text: Es tut mir leid, ich habe keine Zeit.
examples.tr: I’m sorry, I don’t have time.

examples.text: Es tut mir leid, dass ich so spät komme.
Dein Opa ist krank? Oh, es tut mir leid.
examples.tr: Your grandpa is ill? Oh, I’m sorry.

synonyms.nuance: short spoken form
sorry – lighter, for small slips
pardon – polite, slightly old-fashioned

etymology.text: A use of the verb leidtun (“to be sorry”).

pitfalls: mir is dative and changes with the person: es tut ihm leid (he is sorry), es tut uns leid (we are sorry).
Spelling: leid with a small l (es tut mir leid), from the verb leidtun.
subtleties: In speech es is usually dropped: Tut mir leid!
Das tut mir leid often means “I’m sorry to hear that” – sympathy, not guilt.
